chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar who said:

I wrote to al-Askari (peace be upon him): A woman made a will to a man and acknowledged to him a debt of eight thousand dirhams, and likewise whatever household goods she had of wool, hair, similar items, gold, and copper, and all that she had she acknowledged to the executor, and she witnessed her will, and she instructed that two pilgrimages be performed on her behalf from this estate, and a slave-girl be given to her for four hundred dirhams. The woman died and left a husband, so we did not know how to proceed from this and the matter became confused upon us. A scribe mentioned that the woman consulted him, so she asked him to write for her what is valid for this will. He said: It is not valid unless you leave her with your acknowledgment of the debt to him by the testimony of witnesses, and you command him after that to execute what you instruct him to do. So he wrote to him the will on this basis, and she acknowledged to the executor this debt. What is your opinion, may Allah preserve your honor, regarding the jurists before you about this, and inform us of that so that we may act upon it, if Allah wills.

He wrote in his hand: If the debt is sound, well-known, and understood, then the debt is deducted from the principal of the estate, if Allah wills. And if the debt is not true, then what she willed from her third is executed, whether it suffices or does not suffice.

key_terms.إِقْرَارٌ: Acknowledgment or confession of a debt
key_terms.ثُلُثٌ: One-third of the estate, the portion available for bequests

ai.seo_question: How is a deceased woman's debt and bequests handled if the debt's validity is uncertain?
ai.summary: This correspondence from al-Askari (peace be upon him) clarifies the legal mechanism for validating a debt acknowledged in a will during illness, distinguishing between genuine debts deducted from the principal estate and bequests fulfilled from the one-third share. The ruling emphasizes the necessity of the debt being 'well-known' (ma'ruf) to prevent heirs from being unfairly burdened by fabricated obligations, a key principle in Shia inheritance jurisprudence. It provides a practical framework for scribes and judges to verify the authenticity of such claims before executing the deceased's wishes.
